name: Chichen Itza
info: Chichen Itza is a large pre-Columbian Maya city in Yucatán, Mexico, a regional capital of the northern Maya lowlands from about 600 to 1100, known for the Temple of Kukulcán, the Great Ball Court and the Sacred Cenote.

facts.made: Founded by the local Maya of northern Yucatán and later shaped by the Itza, a Maya group of debated origins who arrived from about 800; its architecture mixes Maya styles with styles of central Mexico
facts.form: A city whose densely built core covers at least 5 square kilometres of levelled ground, with stone pyramids, temples, palaces, colonnades and thirteen ball courts, linked by over 80 paved causeways and once painted in red, green, blue and purple
facts.where: Tinúm Municipality, Yucatán, Mexico, between Valladolid and Mérida; federal property in the care of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH), with many objects from the Sacred Cenote at Harvard's Peabody Museum
facts.known: the Temple of Kukulcán (El Castillo) and its equinox shadow serpent; the Great Ball Court; the Sacred Cenote and its offerings; the Caracol; the Temple of the Warriors; Puuc, Chenes and central Mexican styles; a UNESCO World Heritage Site

t: Chichen Itza became the dominant capital of the northern Maya lowlands as the southern centres declined, controlling trade through its port of Isla Cerritos.
Its mix of Maya and central Mexican styles was once read as migration or conquest from central Mexico, but most scholars now see it as cultural diffusion.
The city declined as a regional centre by 1100, yet the Sacred Cenote remained a place of pilgrimage when the Spanish arrived.
dyk: A handclap before the staircase of the Temple of Kukulcán produces an echo that resembles the chirp of a bird, similar to that of the quetzal.
ev: Chichen Itza rose to regional prominence toward the end of the Early Classic period
The earliest hieroglyphic date found at the site was recorded
The city expanded to become a powerful regional capital controlling north and central Yucatán
Chichen Itza declined as a regional centre, before the rise of Mayapan
Francisco de Montejo the Younger, besieged by the Maya, abandoned the city he had renamed Ciudad Real
John Lloyd Stephens's Incidents of Travel in Yucatan brought the site into the popular imagination
Edward Herbert Thompson dredged the Sacred Cenote and shipped most of the finds to Harvard's Peabody Museum
The Mexican government gave the Carnegie Institution a permit for long-term excavation and restoration

sections.origins:
Chichen Itza lies in the east of the Mexican state of Yucatán, on a karst plain where the rivers run underground. Four natural sinkholes, or cenotes, could supply water year round and made the place attractive for settlement; they belong to the Ring of Cenotes formed along the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater. The Maya name means 'At the mouth of the well of the Itzá'. The Chilam Balam books record an earlier name of the Late Classic period, beginning with the word for seven, whose meaning is debated: Uuc Yabnal, 'Seven Great House', is one reading.

The city was founded by the local Maya of northern Yucatán. Another Maya group of debated origins, the Itza, began arriving around 800 and gradually established themselves; their name, given by local people, is said to mean 'those who speak our language brokenly'. Chichen Itza rose to regional prominence toward the end of the Early Classic, roughly 600, and became a major capital late in the Late Classic and early in the Terminal Classic, as the great centres of the southern lowlands declined. Its rise may have contributed to the collapse of its neighbours Yaxuna and Coba in the 10th century.
sections.content:
The site's buildings are grouped in sets once divided by low walls. The Great North Platform holds the Temple of Kukulcán, named for a feathered serpent deity and called El Castillo by the Spanish: a step pyramid about 30 metres high of nine square terraces, with a stairway on each face and a temple on top. Near it stand the Great Ball Court, at 168 by 70 metres the largest and best preserved in ancient Mesoamerica, with rings carved with feathered serpents and panels of ball players, one of them decapitated; the Temples of the Jaguar; a skull platform; the Temple of the Warriors with its rows of carved columns; and the Group of a Thousand Columns.

A causeway 270 metres long leads to the Sacred Cenote, 60 metres across, its water some 27 metres below sheer cliffs. The Osario Group holds a smaller pyramid over a natural cave and the Temple of Xtoloc beside the second great cenote. The Central Group includes Las Monjas, a governmental palace in the Puuc style whose texts often name a ruler called Kʼakʼupakal, the round Caracol, theorised to have been an observatory aligned with the path of Venus, and the Akab Dzib, 'Dark Writing', named for its carved glyphs.
sections.making:
The core of the city was laid out between 750 and 900, and its final layout after 900. Builders levelled the broken terrain for the major groups, with the greatest effort spent on the areas of the Castillo, Las Monjas, the Osario and the Main Southwest group. The earliest hieroglyphic date found at the site is equivalent to 832, and the last, in the Osario, to 998. Many buildings were painted in colours chosen from the pigments most easily found nearby, so the city should be imagined as a colourful place.

Like other Mesoamerican builders, the Maya of Chichen Itza raised larger structures over older ones. Excavation in the mid-1930s found an earlier temple buried inside the Temple of Kukulcán, with a Chac Mool and a red jaguar throne spotted with inlaid jade, and scanning in 2025 showed that this inner pyramid had itself grown through several stages. The Temple of the Warriors likewise encases an older Temple of the Chac Mool. The architecture combines the Puuc and Chenes styles of the northern lowlands, concentrated in Old Chichén and Las Monjas, with forms resembling those of central Mexico; the Temple of the Warriors is analogous to Temple B at the Toltec capital of Tula, built here on a larger scale.
sections.reception:
Chichen Itza was among the largest Maya cities and may have had the most diverse population in the Maya world; it was likely one of the mythical great cities, or Tollans, of later Mesoamerican literature. Through its port at Isla Cerritos it took part in the sea trade around the peninsula, obtaining obsidian from central Mexico and gold from southern Central America, and it drew tribute from cities it conquered. In the late 1980s some archaeologists proposed that a council of elite lineages, a 'multepal', ruled it, a view since called into question in favour of rule by kings.

Post-Conquest Maya and Spanish sources say that objects and people were sacrificed into the Sacred Cenote to the rain god Chaac, especially in times of drought. Thousands of objects have been recovered from it, with skeletons of children, men and women; some show wounds consistent with sacrifice, while others may be non-violent burials, and the Spanish accounts, written long afterwards, may carry colonial biases, so the question remains debated. Colonial sources such as the Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel say Hunac Ceel of Mayapan conquered the city in the 13th century, but the archaeological dating makes that unlikely while Chichen Itza was an active centre.
sections.survival:
Chichen Itza declined as a regional centre by 1100, though the area may not have been abandoned: the Spanish found a thriving local population, and the cenote was still visited by pilgrims. Francisco de Montejo the Younger made the city his capital, Ciudad Real, but the Maya besieged his force, and he abandoned it in 1534; by 1588 the land was a cattle ranch. After Stephens's book of 1843, explorers photographed and described the ruins, and in 1875 Augustus and Alice Le Plongeon excavated the reclining figure he named 'Chaacmol', the origin of the term Chac Mool.

In 1894 the US consul Edward Herbert Thompson bought the hacienda that included the ruins and from 1904 to 1910 dredged the Sacred Cenote, shipping most of the finds to the Peabody Museum. In 1926 Mexico charged him with theft and seized the hacienda; in 1944 its Supreme Court ruled he had broken no laws. The Carnegie Institution restored the Temple of the Warriors and the Caracol from 1923, while the Mexican government restored El Castillo and the Great Ball Court. A 1972 law placed all pre-Columbian monuments under federal ownership, and in 2010 the state of Yucatán bought the land beneath the main monuments.
sections.legacy:
Chichen Itza is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited archaeological sites in Mexico. Tourism there began more than a century ago with Stephens's readers; in 1923 Governor Felipe Carrillo Puerto opened a highway to the ruins, and the Mayaland Hotel followed in 1930. In 2007 the Temple of Kukulcán was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in a vote whose methods were criticised, and the publicity renewed debate in Mexico over who owned the site.

Each spring equinox several thousand visitors gather to watch the triangular shadows that seem to send a serpent down the northern staircase. Some scholars suggest the effect represents Kukulcán, though the idea that it was designed to record the equinox is highly unlikely, since it can be seen for weeks. The monuments can no longer be climbed: access to El Castillo closed in 2006 after a visitor fell to her death. In 2024 a museum of more than 1,000 pieces opened beside the site, reached by the Tren Maya.

summary: Chichen Itza was a Maya city in Yucatán that dominated the northern lowlands from about 600 until it declined by 1100, building pyramids, ball courts and temples in Maya and central Mexican styles around its sacred cenotes. Conquered land under Spain and later dredged and excavated, it is now a World Heritage Site and one of Mexico's most visited ruins.
